questions.question: What are the most important secure coding practices for Java/Spring Boot developers, and how do you bake security into day-to-day coding (not bolt it on later)?
questions.title: Secure Coding for Java/Spring: Input Validation, Output Encoding, Auth, Crypto, Dependencies
questions.direct_answer: Secure coding is about **making the secure path the easy path** — using frameworks, annotations, and patterns that eliminate whole classes of vulnerabilities rather than relying on every developer to remember every rule. For Java/Spring Boot, the non-negotiables are: **parameterize all queries** (JPA / JdbcTemplate; never concat SQL), **validate and constrain input at the boundary** (Bean Validation, size limits, allowlists), **encode output by context** (Thymeleaf auto-escapes HTML; explicit encoding for JSON attributes, URLs, headers), **use Spring Security properly** (`@PreAuthorize`, method security, `SecurityFilterChain` with CSRF, CORS, security headers), **never trust client data** (re-authorize server-side; don't expose internal IDs), **strong crypto via standard libs** (`BCryptPasswordEncoder`, `SecureRandom`, `java.security.KeyStore`; never home-rolled algorithms), **manage secrets in a vault** (never Git/Docker images/logs), and **keep dependencies current** (Dependabot/Renovate + Snyk/OWASP dep-check). Equally critical: **threat-model before coding**, **pair with security in code review**, **add security tests** (SAST via Semgrep/CodeQL, SCA, DAST, authZ tests), and **log security events** without leaking secrets. The biggest real-world wins come from culture: **security as every developer's job**, **champions embedded in teams**, **shift-left** via pre-commit hooks, and **blameless incidents** that teach. Senior engineers' move: turn generic OWASP advice into **codified defaults** (archetype/starter with security baked in, shared filter chain, lint rules) so the right thing happens by default.

interviewer_intent.security: Practical secure coding knowledge in Java/Spring; shift-left mindset; tooling + culture
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating security as checklist at end; home-rolling crypto; client-side authorization; missing output encoding context

sections.title: The Shift-Left Secure Coding Mindset
sections.content:
Security used to be 'scan before release'. Modern teams **shift left**: security becomes part of design, coding, and CI — not a gate at the end.

Why this matters:
- **Cost** of fixing a vulnerability rises sharply the later it's found (IBM SSDLC data: 100x in production vs design phase)
- **Coverage** is better when every engineer owns security, not just AppSec team
- **Velocity** is better when secure patterns are defaults, not exceptions

The architecture of secure coding has two layers:

**1. Codified defaults** (safe by construction)
- Framework choices eliminate whole classes of bugs: JPA parameterizes by default; Thymeleaf escapes HTML; Spring Security enforces authz
- Use them correctly and a lot of risk is gone

**2. Active practices** (safe by discipline)
- Input validation at the boundary, output encoding by context, least privilege, secrets in a vault, current deps, audit logs, threat modeling, security tests

A senior engineer's job isn't to list OWASP Top 10 — it's to make the **right defaults pervasive** and the **wrong patterns impossible or painful**. Archetype repos, shared starter libs, lint rules, code review checklists, CI gates.

sections.title: Input Handling — Validate, Constrain, Parameterize
Output Encoding, AuthN/AuthZ, Crypto, Secrets
sections.content:
**Output encoding by context**

Data safe in one context (HTML body) may be dangerous in another (JavaScript, URL, header). Encode for the exact destination.

- **HTML body**: Thymeleaf `th:text` auto-escapes; React / Angular / Vue escape in JSX templates
- **HTML attributes**: Thymeleaf `th:attr`; for React, ensure value not passed as `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`
- **JavaScript strings** embedded in HTML: use `JavaScriptEscaper` / OWASP Java Encoder `Encode.forJavaScript()`
- **URL path / query**: `URLEncoder.encode(value, UTF_8)`
- **HTTP headers**: strip CR/LF; use framework methods (Spring's `HttpHeaders`), not string concatenation
- **SQL**: parameterize (not encoding)
- **Log messages**: prefer structured logging with placeholders; never format user data into a log line without neutralizing newlines (CRLF log injection)

**Spring Security: Authn and Authz done right**

```java
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true)
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain filter(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.ignoringRequestMatchers("/api/public/**"))
            .headers(h -> h
                .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives("default-src 'self'"))
                .httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts.maxAgeInSeconds(31536000).includeSubDomains(true))
                .frameOptions(HeadersConfigurer.FrameOptionsConfig::deny))
            .cors(cors -> cors.configurationSource(corsConfig()))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health", "/actuator/info").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .build();
    }
}
```

**Method security for authorization**
```java
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER') or #order.ownerId == principal.userId")
public OrderDto getOrder(@P("order") Order order) { ... }
```

Key principles:
- Authorization is **server-side, every request** (don't trust client flags)
- **Fail closed** — deny by default; explicit allow
- Use **direct object reference checks** (not just role): the object owner or principal check prevents IDOR
- **Don't expose internal IDs** (sequential integers); use UUIDs or public slugs
- **Re-check on state-changing operations**; even if UI hides the button

**JWT / session tokens**
- Validate issuer, audience, signature, expiration
- Use short-lived access tokens + refresh tokens
- Store refresh tokens server-side (rotating)
- Never put secrets or PII beyond ID / role in the token

**Strong crypto via standard libraries**

- **Passwords**: `BCryptPasswordEncoder` (work factor 10–12) or `Argon2PasswordEncoder`. Never MD5/SHA1/SHA256.
- **Random**: `SecureRandom` (never `Math.random()` for security-relevant values)
- **Symmetric encryption**: AES-GCM via `javax.crypto.Cipher`; don't use ECB
- **Asymmetric**: Java's `KeyPairGenerator`; RSA 2048+ or Ed25519
- **HMAC**: `Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256")`
- **TLS**: default JDK config; ensure minimum TLS 1.2; no custom TrustManagers that accept all certs
- **Key storage**: `java.security.KeyStore` + HSM/KMS in production
- **Never**: roll your own crypto; use hard-coded IVs; reuse keys across contexts

**Secrets management**
- Secrets live in a **vault** (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault)
- Mounted into pods via CSI driver or External Secrets Operator; loaded via Spring Cloud Config
- **Never** in Git, container images, application logs, or environment files committed to VCS
- Rotate regularly; prefer **dynamic secrets** where possible (Vault DB credentials)
- `.gitignore` + pre-commit hooks (gitleaks) prevent accidental commits

sections.title: Dependencies, CI Gates, Testing, and Culture
sections.content:
**Keep dependencies current**

- **Dependabot / Renovate**: automated PRs for updates
- **Snyk / OWASP Dependency-Check**: vulnerability scanning in CI
- **SBOM** (Software Bill of Materials) generated (`syft`, `cyclonedx-maven-plugin`)
- Track **Maven BOMs** to pin consistent versions across the org
- Quarterly 'upgrade sprints' for major bumps; continuous automated for minor/patch
- Treat **transitive deps** as yours — they're in your binary
- **Evaluate before adding** a new dep: maintenance, security history, alternatives

**CI / CD security gates**

- **SAST**: Semgrep, SonarQube, CodeQL, SpotBugs-Find-Sec-Bugs — block on high-severity
- **SCA**: Snyk / Dependabot scoring + policy (fail on CVSS ≥ 7)
- **Secret scanning**: gitleaks / trufflehog pre-commit + CI
- **Container scanning**: Trivy / Grype for base images and final images
- **IaC scanning**: checkov, tfsec, Terrascan for Terraform/Kubernetes
- **DAST**: OWASP ZAP / Burp against staging for runtime issues
- **Policy as code**: OPA / Conftest for K8s manifests

Fail the build on critical; create tickets with SLAs for lower severity. Don't let the queue grow.

**Security testing as part of the suite**

- Unit tests for auth/authz logic
- Integration tests with `@WithMockUser` / Keycloak Testcontainers
- Contract tests for AuthN error paths (401, 403)
- Property-based tests for input validation
- `@SpringBootTest` verifying security headers, CSRF, CORS behave as configured
- **Negative tests**: explicitly assert unauthorized access is rejected; don't only test happy paths

```java
@Test
@WithMockUser(roles = "USER")
void nonAdminCannotAccessAdminEndpoint() throws Exception {
    mockMvc.perform(get("/admin/users"))
           .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
}
```

**Threat modeling (STRIDE, Data Flow Diagrams)**

Before coding a new feature:
- Identify trust boundaries
- Enumerate threats per STRIDE category (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info Disclosure, DoS, Elevation)
- Decide mitigations (prevent, detect, transfer, accept)
- Document in the design doc; review with security champion

Light-touch threat modeling (30 minutes per feature) catches more than most scans.

**Logging and monitoring**
- Log security-relevant events: auth failures, authz denials, suspicious patterns
- **Never log** passwords, tokens, secrets, PII in plaintext
- Structured logs with correlation IDs; central SIEM (Splunk, Elastic, Datadog Security)
- Alert on anomalies (spike in 401s, credential stuffing signatures)

**Culture and process**

- **Security champions**: embed one engineer per team with security training as the liaison to the security org
- **Blameless incident culture**: postmortems teach; punishment silences
- **Shift left via tooling**: pre-commit hooks prevent, SAST in IDE catches early
- **Security-focused code review**: checklists for auth, input, secrets
- **Archetype repos** with security baked in (filter chain, logging, dep scanning); new services inherit
- **Regular training**: OWASP Top 10 refreshers; internal 'attack' walkthroughs of real incidents
- **Red team / purple team exercises**: real-world validation

**Common anti-patterns**

1. **Home-rolled crypto** — 'it's just a little XOR' is always wrong
2. **Client-side authz** — hiding a button ≠ authorizing the action
3. **Trusting internal traffic** — zero-trust: authenticate internal calls too
4. **Secrets in env vars committed to Git** — .env files in repos
5. **Logging sensitive data** — passwords, card numbers, tokens end up in log files
6. **Disabling CSRF / CORS without understanding** — common 'make it work' shortcut
7. **Bypass patterns in code** ('if dev env, skip auth') that leak to prod
8. **Security last** — threat-model and scan after feature is 'done'; expensive to fix
9. **Security by obscurity** — hiding endpoints is not protecting them
10. **Ignoring SAST / SCA queue** — piles up; nobody triages; real vulns buried

sections.title: Pragmatic Trade-offs and Defense-in-Depth
sections.content:
**Defense in depth**
- No single layer is perfect; stack controls
- WAF catches some injection + rate limits before your app
- App layer: validation + parameterized queries
- DB layer: least-privilege user; row-level security where applicable
- Audit layer: detection + alerting
- Compensating controls: even if one layer fails, others catch

**Security vs velocity**
- Over-locked-down dev environments slow everyone; minimal, realistic dev data, quick auth bypass via `@WithMockUser` in tests, but never in prod
- Security gates should be **fast** (SAST < 5 min; SCA < 3 min) — or devs will find workarounds
- Automate everything you can; manual security review only where automation can't

**Security vs user experience**
- Sign-in friction: MFA balanced with trusted-device recognition
- Rate limits tuned to legitimate traffic
- Password policies: NIST SP 800-63B (length > complexity; check against breached-password lists)
- Consider passkeys / WebAuthn for reduced friction with better security

**Build vs buy**
- Auth: use OAuth2 / OIDC / OpenID Connect providers (Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, AWS Cognito) unless you're an identity company
- Secrets: managed vaults
- WAF: Cloudflare, AWS WAF — not your app's problem

**Public API vs internal API security**
- Public APIs need WAF, rate limiting, CAPTCHA, strong authn, DDoS protection
- Internal APIs: mTLS + short-lived tokens + network policies
- Zero-trust: don't assume internal = safe

**GDPR / compliance interactions**
- Data minimization: store less, less to leak
- Encryption at rest and in transit
- Right-to-erasure: clear retention policies and operationalized deletion
- Audit trails: who accessed what, when

**When to escalate to security org**
- Pre-design of sensitive features (payments, auth, PII)
- When a scan flags something you don't understand
- When a third-party library has a disclosed CVE affecting you
- Before adding a new dep or service to the stack
- Any suspected incident — err on the side of reporting

**Operational resilience**
- Assume breach — design for detection and containment
- Least privilege everywhere (IAM, K8s RBAC, service accounts)
- Network segmentation (VPC, security groups, namespace-level NetworkPolicies)
- Backup + DR strategy for security incidents (ransomware)
- Incident response runbooks rehearsed in game days

**Senior engineer moves**
- **Build security capabilities into the platform** — archetype, shared libs, defaults
- **Codify security knowledge** — internal wiki, ADRs for security decisions, training content
- **Ship to the easy path** — if the safe way requires 10 lines and the unsafe way 2, safe will lose
- **Partner with security, don't outsource thinking** — engineers are closer to the code than any scanner
- **Lead threat modeling** sessions for your team
- **Use incidents as learning** — write blameless postmortems that the whole engineering org reads
- **Balance signal and noise** in security tooling — too many false positives and everyone ignores all alerts
- **Champion shift-left** — every layer earlier is cheaper

**Strategic take**
- Secure coding is **culture + defaults + discipline**, not a checklist
- Framework defaults (Spring Security, JPA, Thymeleaf) eliminate most risk if used correctly
- Shift left: threat model → code → SAST/SCA → tests → DAST → runtime monitoring
- Senior engineers make the secure path the easy path and create a culture where every engineer owns security

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Make the **secure path the easy path**; use framework defaults (Spring Security, JPA, Bean Validation, Thymeleaf) correctly
- **Validate input at boundary** with Bean Validation; constrain size, format, allowlists
- **Parameterize all queries** (JPA, JdbcTemplate); never concat user input into SQL/JPQL
- **Encode output by context** (HTML body, attribute, JS, URL, header); OWASP Java Encoder for tricky cases
- **Server-side authz** with `@PreAuthorize`, `SecurityFilterChain`; fail closed; prevent IDOR
- **Strong crypto via standard libs**: BCrypt, SecureRandom, AES-GCM; no home-rolled
- **Secrets in a vault**; never in Git/images/logs; rotate regularly; prefer dynamic
- **Keep deps current**: Dependabot/Renovate + Snyk/OWASP dep-check; SBOM; BOMs
- **CI gates**: SAST (Semgrep/CodeQL), SCA (Snyk), secret scan (gitleaks), container scan (Trivy), IaC scan
- **Security tests** for authz, headers, CSRF; negative tests essential
- **Threat model** 30 min per feature before coding
- **Audit logs** for security events; never log secrets/PII in plaintext
- **Culture**: security champions, shift-left, blameless incidents, codified defaults

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Secure coding is about making the secure path the easy path — using frameworks, annotations, and patterns that eliminate whole classes of vulnerabilities rather than relying on every developer to remember every rule.

**For Java/Spring Boot non-negotiables**
- Parameterize all queries (JPA/JdbcTemplate; never concat SQL)

- Strong crypto via standard libs (BCryptPasswordEncoder, SecureRandom, java.security.KeyStore; never home-rolled)
- Manage secrets in a vault (never Git/Docker images/logs)
- Keep dependencies current (Dependabot/Renovate + Snyk/OWASP dep-check)

**Equally critical**
- Threat-model before coding
- Pair with security in code review
- Add security tests (SAST via Semgrep/CodeQL, SCA, DAST, authZ tests)
- Log security events without leaking secrets

**Real-world wins come from culture**
- Security as every developer's job
- Champions embedded in teams
- Shift-left via pre-commit hooks
- Blameless incidents that teach

**Senior engineer move**
- Turn generic OWASP advice into codified defaults
- Archetype/starter with security baked in, shared filter chain, lint rules

**Shift-left mindset**

- Modern: part of design, coding, CI — not a gate at end
- Cost rises 100x in prod vs design (IBM SSDLC)
- Coverage better when every engineer owns security
- Velocity better when secure patterns are defaults

**Two layers**
- Codified defaults (safe by construction): JPA parameterizes; Thymeleaf escapes; Spring Security enforces
- Active practices (safe by discipline): validation, encoding, least privilege, vault, current deps, audit logs, threat modeling, tests

**Input handling**

*Validate at boundary*
- Bean Validation (Jakarta) on DTOs
- @NotBlank @Size @NotNull @Positive @Email @Pattern @Valid
- Nested validation on collections
- @Valid triggers; violations → 400 with structured error
- Handles null/blank/empty, size/length bounds (prevents payload bombs), format, ranges

*Constrain aggressively*
- Always size-limit strings, collections, byte payloads
- Reject unexpected fields (fail-on-unknown-properties=true)
- Allowlists (enums, Pattern) not denylists
- Business invariants in domain layer, not just syntactic

*Parameterize queries — always*
- JPA: @Query with :param; never concat
- JdbcTemplate/JdbcClient: ? placeholders
- Dynamic: Criteria API or Specifications, not string building

*Other injection contexts*
- LDAP: escape; LdapTemplate with param binding
- OS command: avoid Runtime.exec('sh -c'); ProcessBuilder with array + allowlist
- XML/XPath: disable DTDs (XXE); IS_SUPPORTING_EXTERNAL_ENTITIES=false
- Template (FreeMarker/Velocity/Thymeleaf): never compile from user input

*File handling*
- Canonicalize paths (Paths.toRealPath); reject .. traversal
- Restrict types/sizes; verify magic bytes, not extension
- Store outside webroot; serve via controlled endpoint with authz

*Deserialization*
- Jackson: avoid polymorphic on arbitrary types; @JsonTypeInfo with allowlist TypeIdResolver or sealed hierarchies
- Java serialization: avoid; if needed ObjectInputFilter to restrict

**Output encoding by context**
- Data safe in one context dangerous in another
- HTML body: Thymeleaf th:text auto-escapes; React/Angular/Vue escape in templates
- HTML attributes: th:attr; avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML
- JavaScript strings in HTML: OWASP Java Encoder Encode.forJavaScript()
- URL: URLEncoder.encode(value, UTF_8)
- HTTP headers: strip CR/LF; framework methods not concat
- SQL: parameterize (not encoding)
- Log messages: structured placeholders; neutralize newlines (CRLF log injection)

**Spring Security authn/authz**
- @EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled=true)
- SecurityFilterChain bean configures: CSRF, security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options), CORS, authorize rules (permitAll/authenticated/hasRole), session STATELESS, oauth2ResourceServer.jwt
- Method security: @PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER') or #order.ownerId == principal.userId")

*Key principles*
- Authz server-side every request (don't trust client flags)
- Fail closed: deny by default; explicit allow
- Direct object reference checks (not just role): prevents IDOR
- Don't expose internal IDs (sequential ints); use UUIDs/slugs
- Re-check on state-changing ops even if UI hides button

*JWT/session tokens*
- Validate issuer, audience, signature, expiration
- Short-lived access + refresh tokens
- Store refresh tokens server-side (rotating)
- Never secrets/PII beyond ID/role in token

**Strong crypto**
- Passwords: BCryptPasswordEncoder (work factor 10-12) or Argon2PasswordEncoder; never MD5/SHA1/SHA256
- Random: SecureRandom; never Math.random() for security
- Symmetric: AES-GCM via javax.crypto.Cipher; no ECB
- Asymmetric: KeyPairGenerator; RSA 2048+ or Ed25519
- HMAC: Mac.getInstance('HmacSHA256')
- TLS: default JDK; min TLS 1.2; no custom TrustManagers accepting all certs
- Key storage: KeyStore + HSM/KMS in prod
- Never: roll own; hard-coded IVs; reuse keys across contexts

**Secrets management**
- Vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault)
- Mounted via CSI driver or External Secrets Operator; loaded via Spring Cloud Config
- Never in Git, images, logs, env files in VCS
- Rotate; prefer dynamic (Vault DB credentials)
- .gitignore + pre-commit hooks (gitleaks) prevent accidents

**Dependencies current**
- Dependabot/Renovate: automated update PRs
- Snyk/OWASP Dependency-Check: scanning in CI
- SBOM (syft, cyclonedx-maven-plugin)
- Maven BOMs pin consistent versions
- Quarterly upgrade sprints for major; continuous automated for minor/patch
- Treat transitive as yours
- Evaluate before adding: maintenance, security history, alternatives

**CI/CD gates**
- SAST: Semgrep, SonarQube, CodeQL, SpotBugs-Find-Sec-Bugs; block on high severity
- SCA: Snyk/Dependabot scoring + policy (fail on CVSS ≥7)
- Secret scanning: gitleaks/trufflehog pre-commit + CI
- Container scanning: Trivy/Grype
- IaC scanning: checkov, tfsec, Terrascan
- DAST: OWASP ZAP/Burp against staging
- Policy as code: OPA/Conftest for K8s
- Fail build on critical; tickets with SLAs for lower; don't let queue grow

**Security testing**
- Unit for auth/authz logic
- Integration with @WithMockUser/Keycloak Testcontainers
- Contract for AuthN error paths (401, 403)
- Property-based for input validation
- @SpringBootTest verifying headers, CSRF, CORS
- Negative tests: assert unauthorized rejected; don't only test happy paths

- Enumerate threats per STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Info Disclosure, DoS, Elevation)

**Logging/monitoring**

- Never log passwords/tokens/secrets/PII plaintext
- Structured logs + correlation IDs; central SIEM (Splunk, Elastic, Datadog Security)
- Alert on anomalies (spike in 401s, credential stuffing signatures)

**Culture**
- Security champions: one engineer per team with training as liaison
- Blameless incident culture: postmortems teach; punishment silences
- Shift left via tooling: pre-commit hooks prevent, SAST in IDE catches early
- Security-focused code review: checklists for auth, input, secrets

1. Home-rolled crypto ('just a little XOR' always wrong)
2. Client-side authz (hiding button ≠ authorizing)

4. Secrets in env vars committed
5. Logging sensitive data
6. Disabling CSRF/CORS without understanding
7. Bypass patterns ('if dev, skip auth') leaking to prod

**Defense in depth**

- WAF catches injection + rate limits

- Audit: detection + alerting

- Build vs buy: OAuth2/OIDC providers (Keycloak, Okta, Auth0, Cognito); managed vaults; managed WAF
- Public vs internal: public needs WAF, rate limits, CAPTCHA; internal mTLS + short tokens + network policies; zero-trust

- Right-to-erasure operationalized

- Pre-design sensitive features (payments, auth, PII)

**Operational resilience**

**Strategic take**
- Secure coding is culture + defaults + discipline, not checklist
- Framework defaults eliminate most risk if used correctly
- Shift left: threat model → code → SAST/SCA → tests → DAST → runtime monitoring
- Seniors make secure path the easy path; culture where every engineer owns security

**Bottom line**
- Best security comes from many small correct defaults, not one big review
- Spring Security + JPA + Bean Validation + Thymeleaf + BCrypt + Vault + Dependabot + Semgrep is the core stack
- Add threat modeling, security tests, blameless postmortems, and champions — security becomes pervasive, not ceremonial

speakable_v2.hook: Secure coding is about making the secure path the easy path — using frameworks, annotations, and patterns that eliminate whole classes of vulnerabilities rather than relying on every developer to remember every rule.

beats.text: Security used to be 'scan before release'. Modern teams shift left: security becomes part of design, coding, and CI — not a gate at the end. Why this matters: Cost of fixing a vulnerability rises sharply the later it's found (IBM SSDLC data: 100x in production vs design phase) Coverage is better when every engineer owns security, not just AppSec team Velocity is better when secure patterns are defaults, not exceptions The architecture of secure coding has two layers: 1. Codified defaults (safe by construction) Framework choices eliminate whole classes.

steps: Validate at the boundary (controller / API layer) Use Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation) on DTOs: ``java public record CreateOrderRequest( @NotBlank @Size(max = 100) String customerRef, @NotNull @Positive BigDecimal amount, @Email String contactEmail, @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]{3}") String currency, @Size(max = 50) @Valid List<OrderLine> lines) {} @PostMapping("/orders") public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest req) { ...
} ` @Valid triggers validation; violations return 400 with structured error.

This handles: Null / blank / empty Size / length bounds (prevents payload bombs) Format (email, regex, URL) Numeric ranges Nested validation on collections Constrain aggressively Always size-limit strings (@Size(max = N)), collections (@Size(max = N) on List), and byte payloads Reject unexpected fields (spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true) Use allowlists (enums, Pattern) not denylists for categorical input Validate business invariants in the domain layer, not just syntactic constraints Parameterize database queries — always JPA/Hibernate: `java // GOOD: parameterized @Query("select.

items: Make the secure path the easy path; use framework defaults (Spring Security, JPA, Bean Validation, Thymeleaf) correctly Validate input at boundary with Bean Validation; constrain size, format, allowlists Parameterize all queries (JPA, JdbcTemplate); never concat user input into SQL/JPQL Encode output by context (HTML body, attribute, JS, URL, header); OWASP Java Encoder for tricky cases Server-side authz with @PreAuthorize, SecurityFilterChain; fail closed; prevent IDOR Strong crypto via standard libs: BCrypt, SecureRandom, AES-GCM; no home-rolled Secrets in a vault; never in Git/images/logs; rotate regularly; prefer dynamic Keep deps current: Dependabot/Renovate + Snyk/OWASP dep-check; SBOM; BOMs CI gates: SAST (Semgrep/CodeQL), SCA (Snyk), secret scan (gitleaks), container scan (Trivy), IaC scan Security tests for authz, headers, CSRF; negative tests essential Threat model 30 min per feature before coding Audit logs for security events; never log secrets/PII in plaintext Culture: security champions, shift-left, blameless incidents, codified defaults

beats.text: Treating security as checklist at end; home-rolling crypto; client-side authorization; missing output encoding context
